newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Britain, China agree on Hong Kong handover details.
newsitem.headline: Britain, China agree on Hong Kong handover details.

text.p: Britain and China reached agreement on Thursday on arrangements for a handover ceremony in Hong Kong around midnight next June 30, when the colony reverts to Chinese rule, British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said.

He also told a news conference after a long meeting with Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen that Chinese Vice-Premier Li Lanqing would visit Britain in November and that agreement had been reached on the establishment of a large British consulate-general in Hong Kong after the Chinese takeover.

The joint handover ceremony would take place in the ground foyer of the new extension to the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre, which has a capacity of over 4,000 people, in the presence of high-level guests including representatives of overseas governments and international organisations.

"This will be a very important occasion, both as a symbol but also representing the joint will of the British and Chinese governments with regard to smooth and successful transition and one which will meet the aspirations of the people of Hong Kong," he added.
The ambassadors of a joint British-Chinese liaison group would sign a document in Hong Kong on Friday detailing the arrangements.
"It is automatic that the governor (Chris Patten) would be part of the ceremony," Rifkind said, though that was not discussed with Qian.
It was not yet known who would be coming from Britain "but you can certainly assume that the level of British representation will correspond to the importance of the occasion," he added.
He also informed Qian that Britain would stage a purely British ceremony at sunset on June 30 on Hong Kong's central waterfront.

"We envisage a dignified ceremony incorporating both civilian and military elements. Hong Kong and Britain are part of each other's history and it's right therefore to commemorate that fact in this important way," he added.
The consulate general in Hong Kong, with a staff of about 180, would be the largest British consulate general anywhere in the world and larger than many embassies.
This would emphasise "the massive interest and commitment of the United Kingdom to Hong Kong in the years to come," the foreign secretary said.

Rifkind and Qian, during their nearly two-hour meeting, reiterated their opposing views about China's intention to establish a provisional legislature as a stop-gap measure until new elections are held in Hong Kong.

"I emphasised our continuing belief that the establishment of such a provisional legislature was both unnecessary and undesirable. The Chinese side responded on the basis of their known positions," Rifkind said.
On other issues, he said he raised with Qian the question of a number of Hong Kong residents detained in China and handed over an updated list.
"We have urged that the Chinese should deal with these matters in a sensitive way and one that respects proper legal obligations."
Rifkind told a questioner the question of Tibet was not raised though he noted he met the Dalai Lama when he visited Britain some weeks ago.
